beats.text: How many people need to be in a room for a fifty-fifty chance that two share a birthday?
Three hundred sixty-five days. No twins, no leap years.
Lock in your answer. Three. Two. One.
The gut says half the year: about one hundred and eighty.
Because everyone gets compared with everyone. Twenty-three people make two hundred fifty-three pairs.
At seventy people, a match is almost certain.
If you guessed way higher, your gut counted people, not pairs.

sources: Birthday problem (standard probability result, e.g. Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1): P(at least one shared birthday among n people, 365 equally likely days) = 1 − 365!/((365−n)!·365^n). n = 22: 47.6 %, n = 23: 50.7 %, n = 70: 99.9 %. Pairs among 23 people: 23·22/2 = 253. Computed in render.py.
Simplification stated in the video: 365 equally likely birthdays, no leap day, no twins. Real birthdays are slightly uneven, which makes a match a little more likely, not less.
